questions.text:
Consider an enterprise network with two Ethernet segments, a web server and a firewall, connected via three routers as shown below.

What is the number of subnets inside the enterprise network?
questions.solution:
Every link between router interfaces (and every LAN behind a router) is a separate subnet:
1. Firewall - left router
2. Firewall - top router
3. Top router - web server
4. Top router - right router
5. Left router - left Ethernet
6. Right router - right Ethernet

Answer: 6

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- A subset of an RE language need not be recursive (e.g. the halting language is a subset of [latex]\Sigma^*[/latex]) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- If [latex]L[/latex] and [latex]\bar L[/latex] are both RE, run both recognizers in parallel; one must accept, so [latex]L[/latex] is recursive [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Every CFL is recursive and recursive languages are closed under complement [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]L_1\cap L_2[/latex] is regular, and every regular language is deterministic context-free [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Every subset of a recursively enumerable language is recursive.
If a language [latex]L[/latex] and its complement [latex]\bar{L}[/latex] are both recursively enumerable, then [latex]L[/latex] must be recursive.
Complement of a context-free language must be recursive.
If [latex]L_1[/latex] and [latex]L_2[/latex] are regular, then [latex]L_1 \cap L_2 [/latex]must be deterministic context-free.

questions.text: Let WB and WT be two set associative cache organizations that use LRU algorithm for cache block replacement. WB is a write back cache and WT is a write through cache. Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.solution:
Check each statement (we need the FALSE ones):
- "Each block in WB and WT has a dirty bit": WT writes memory on every write, so it needs no dirty bit [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- "Every write hit in WB transfers data to memory": WB only sets the dirty bit; memory is updated on eviction [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- "Eviction from WT causes no transfer to memory": memory is already up to date [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "A read miss in WB never evicts a dirty block": the LRU victim can be dirty [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Each cache block in WB and WT has a dirty bit.
Every write hit in WB leads to a data transfer from cache to main memory.
Eviction of a block from WT will not lead to data transfer from cache to main memory.
A read miss in WB will never lead to eviction of a dirty block from WB.

questions.text:
Consider the following three relations in a relational database.
[latex]Employee(eId, Name), Brand (bId, bName), Own(eId ,bId)[/latex]
Which of the following relational algebra expressions return the set of [latex]eIds[/latex] who own all the brands?
questions.solution:
"Owns all brands" is relational division by the set of all brands.

- Option 1: [latex]\Pi_{eId,bId}(Own)\div\Pi_{bId}(Brand)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] exactly division [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 2: [latex]\Pi_{eId}(Own)\times\Pi_{bId}(Brand)[/latex] lists every (employee, brand) pair; subtracting Own leaves the pairs an employee does not own. Removing those employees leaves those who own every brand [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (this is the expansion of division).
- Option 3 divides by [latex]\Pi_{bId}(Own)[/latex] (brands owned by someone); a brand owned by nobody would be ignored [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- Option 4 divides a full cross product, which returns every employee [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.

Answer: Options 1 and 2
